analysis.title: US Weekly Kickstart: One step back from the retail trader, two steps forward from household equity demand
key_insights: Hedge fund derisking was sharp this week. The Hedge Fund VIP long/short basket pair fell 4.2% on Thursday (Oct 22), a one-day decline matched in the past decade only on DeepSeek Monday in January 2025 and the March 2020 COVID sell-off.

GS Prime Services data show a large decline in hedge fund gross leverage, though gross leverage remains above the 90th percentile vs. the past 5 years. Fundamental hedge fund net leverage is close to 5-year lows.

Retail trading rose modestly in the past two weeks, but retail volumes are down about 20% since mid-summer and more than 40% since late 2025. Retail is 9% of total US equity volumes, down from 15% late last year and close to the lowest level since 2020.

Leveraged ETFs show a buy-the-dip pattern. Retail's share of trading in leveraged index ETFs is roughly double its share in unleveraged ETFs tracking the same indices, and inflows surged over the past two weeks, which fits the usual inverse relation between flows and returns.

Monthly prediction market volumes grew to $78 billion in September from $5 billion a year ago. September was helped by seasonal sports volume and the upcoming US elections. Robinhood data show retail options trading nearly doubled over the past year.

GS attributes most of this year's drop in retail trading to weak consumer sentiment and rising energy prices. GS economists estimate 2026 real income growth at only 1%, with spending supported by a lower personal saving rate. They expect real income growth to improve in 2027 as inflation moderates.

The Speculative Trading Indicator (volumes in unprofitable stocks, penny stocks and stocks with EV/sales above 10x) surged in mid-2025 to its highest level in decades outside 1998-2001 and 2020-2021. It now ranks in the 80th percentile since 1995 and sits below late-2025 and summer-2026 levels. Margin balances at the largest retail brokers are very elevated vs. history but have not risen since June.

Retail trading assets are a small part of household equity exposure. The $12 trillion in self-directed brokerage accounts is about 18% of the $65 trillion of household equity assets, direct and indirect.
Households directly own 42% of the US corporate equity market and own the majority including indirect holdings through retirement accounts, mutual funds and ETFs.

Households bought $840 billion of US equities in H1 2026 per Federal Reserve data. YTD inflows to US equity funds total $350 billion and remain robust in recent months. This more than offset weaker corporate demand.

US corporates issued a net $175 billion of equities in H1 2026. Including expiring lockups, GS expects net public equity supply next year to rise by the largest amount since 2000, so household demand will be needed to absorb it.

Labor market and interest rates are the key drivers of 2027 household demand. Historically, flows into equity funds improve after rises in household net worth and falls in unemployment and perceived recession risk, and are inversely related to yields on cash and bonds. GS's baseline of a stable labor market and modestly lower yields is supportive.

The top 10% of households by wealth own 87% of household equity assets. Demand from the wealthiest households has likely been helped by liquid wealth from large public offerings, which GS expects to remain a tailwind.

Household equity allocation is a record 55% of financial assets. Historically the allocation tracks equity valuations closely. Interest rates and AI-related disruption are among the top factors affecting it, while the shift in retirement assets is a tailwind: 401(k) assets rose from 13% of the US retirement market in 1995 to 21% today.

S&P 500 forecasts: GS year-end 2026 target 8000 (about 4% above the 7663 level) and 12-month target 8700 (about 14%). GS EPS is $375 for 2026, $415 for 2027 and $460 for 2028, vs. bottom-up consensus of $367, $426 and $494. Forward P/E is 19x.

Q3 2026 earnings season so far (122 S&P 500 companies reported, 24% of the index by count, 25% by cap): 57% of equal-weighted companies beat on EPS and 10% missed. Cap-weighted, Information Technology is the strongest sector with 83% beating, and Communication Services is weakest with 26% beating and 73% missing.

Sector moves this week: Consumer Staples (+3.7%), Utilities (+2.9%) and Financials (+2.6%) led. Communication Services (-7.2%) and Information Technology (-3.1%) lagged, led by Semiconductors (-5.4%) and Media & Entertainment (-7.9%). The S&P 500 fell 1.0% while the equal-weight index rose 1.5%.

Largest S&P 500 decliners this week included Howmet (-16%), Flex (-15%), Quanta (-14%), Lam Research (-13%), Bloom Energy (-13%), KLA (-12%) and GE Vernova (-12%). Leaders included Hasbro (+19%), Charles River (+15%), Roper (+14%), Allegion (+14%) and CrowdStrike (+13%).

Thematic baskets this week: Long vs. Short Duration -10.2%, Strong vs. Weak Balance Sheet -6.0%, Hedge Fund VIP -6.7%, Interest Rate Sensitive -5.6%, EM Sales -5.2%, Dual Beta -5.0%. Mutual Fund Over- vs. Underweights +4.3% and Dividend Growth +2.2%.

GS macro forecasts: US 10-year yield 5.0% now, 4.8% in 3 months, 4.7% in 6 months and 4.5% in 12 months. Brent is $113 now with a 12-month target of $75. S&P 500 12-month target is 8700. COMEX gold is $4060 with a 12-month target of $5140.

GS US Equity Sentiment Indicator reads -0.2 z-score, between the stretched (above 1.0) and light (below -1.0) thresholds. Trailing 12-month fund flows: equities $373 billion, money markets $480 billion, bonds $833 billion.

earnings_insights: Q3 2026 season as of October 23 (122 S&P 500 companies, 24% of the index by count): 57% beat on EPS (equal-weighted), 10% negative, 32% in-line, average surprise 5%. Revenue: 40% positive, 18% negative, average surprise 1%.
Cap-weighted Q3 2026 (25% of index weight reported): 50% positive EPS surprises, 18% negative, 31% in-line. Revenue: 46% positive, 10% negative.
Comparative full-season EPS beat rates: 69% in 2Q 2026, 65% in 1Q 2026, 55% in 4Q 2025 and 66% in 3Q 2025.

GS S&P 500 adjusted EPS forecast is $375 for 2026E (+36% y/y) and $415 for 2027E (+11%), vs. bottom-up consensus of $367 (+33%) and $426 (+16%) and top-down strategist consensus of $356 (+30%) and $410 (+15%).
GS top-down 2026 EPS contributions: Info Tech $118 (+68% y/y), Comm Services $48 (+64%), Energy $21 (+82%). Consensus bottom-up Info Tech is $114 for 2026 and $161 for 2027.
Info Tech reported the strongest cap-weighted EPS beat rate among sectors at 83%. Comm Services cap-weighted was 26% positive and 73% negative.

macro_indicators.interpretation: GS economists expect weak real income growth, with spending supported by a lower saving rate. They expect improvement in 2027 as inflation moderates.
The saving rate has declined, which has helped sustain consumer spending despite weak income growth.
GS expects yields to fall modestly, which supports household equity demand.
Elevated energy prices are weighing on consumer sentiment and retail trading.

risk_factors: Weak consumer sentiment, elevated gasoline prices and inflation weigh on real income and retail trading.
Rising net equity supply: next year's net supply of US public equity is expected to rise by the largest amount since 2000, so household demand must absorb it.
Labor market deterioration or higher yields on cash and bonds would reduce household equity demand.
AI-related disruption and the path of interest rates are key uncertainties for household equity allocation, now at a record 55% of financial assets.
Demand is concentrated: the top 10% of households own 87% of household equity assets, so aggregate demand depends on wealthy households.
Recent macro volatility is a reminder of risk around the baseline forecasts of solid 2027 household demand.

tension_points.bull_case: A stable labor market and modestly lower yields in GS's baseline support solid household demand in 2027. Households bought $840 billion of US equities in H1 2026 and fund inflows are $350 billion YTD. The secular rise in 401(k) equity allocations and wealth from large public offerings add support.
tension_points.bear_case: Net public equity supply is expected to rise next year by the largest amount since 2000, and household allocation is already a record 55%. Labor market weakness, higher cash and bond yields, or AI-related disruption could cut demand, and ownership is concentrated in the top 10% of households.
tension_points.what_invalidates: A deterioration in the labor market (rising unemployment) or higher yields on cash and bonds, which historically are followed by weaker equity fund flows.
